status_summary: A DHS final rule published 2025-09-05 (effective 2025-10-06) codifies law-enforcement authorities that the Homeland Security Secretary delegated to the USCIS Director in May 2025, covering investigations, warrants, arrests and firearms; it was issued without notice and comment. An interim final rule effective 2025-10-30 (90 FR 48799) ended automatic extensions of expiring work permits for renewals filed on or after that date, citing vetting; DHS adopted it without change as a final rule published and effective 2026-10-14 (91 FR 65306), after a federal court in California (Jane Doe v. Department of Homeland Security, No. 8:26-cv-00060) ruled on 2026-09-11, per Bloomberg Law, that DHS had not justified skipping notice and comment, with relief limited to seven plaintiffs. An interim final rule published 2026-04-29 (FR document 2026-08333, corrected 2026-07-21) codifies provisions of the 2025 reconciliation law (H.R. 1), including new asylum-related fees and a limit on the validity period of certain work permits (for TPS holders, one year or the period of status, per a Federal Register search excerpt of the rule). Three proposed rules were not final as of 2026-10-17 as far as found: universal biometrics collection with no age limit and a DNA option (published 2025-11-03, comments closed 2026-01-02), limits on work permits for asylum applicants (2026-02-23, comments closed 2026-04-24), and stricter discretionary work permits for parolees, deferred-action recipients and people on orders of supervision (2026-06-05, comments closed 2026-08-04). On 2025-06-11 the Justice Department's Civil Division issued a memorandum, Civil Division Enforcement Priorities, whose section 5 directs the division to pursue denaturalization cases where the law and evidence permit, listing ten priority categories; restructuring of the fraud directorate, FLETC training and a standing denaturalization unit were not verified.

timeline.event: Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate issues the Civil Division memorandum Civil Division Enforcement Priorities. Section 5, Prioritizing Denaturalization, directs the division to pursue denaturalization cases where the law permits and the evidence supports them, and lists ten priority categories (including national security threats, human rights abuses, criminal gang activity and fraud against the United States) that are not exhaustive or ranked. The memo is a DOJ action; it does not describe a USCIS unit.
timeline.source: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Division

timeline.event: DHS publishes a final rule, effective 2025-10-06, codifying law-enforcement authorities delegated to the USCIS Director in May 2025 (investigations, search and arrest warrants, arrests, use of force, firearms), issued without notice and comment under the exception for agency organization and procedure.

DHS publishes, effective immediately, an interim final rule ending automatic extension of expiring employment authorization documents for renewal applications filed on or after this date (previously up to 540 days), citing the need to finish vetting first; comments were due 2025-12-01.

USCIS proposes to require biometrics from anyone filing or associated with a benefit request unless exempted (including citizens and permanent residents), remove age limits, define biometrics to include DNA, limit reuse of earlier biometrics, and allow continuous vetting until naturalization; 6,661 comments were received by the 2026-01-02 deadline.

DHS proposes work-permit changes for asylum applicants: pause accepting applications when affirmative asylum processing exceeds 180 days, lengthen the waiting period to 365 days, and add eligibility criteria; comments closed 2026-04-24.

DHS publishes an interim final rule, USCIS Immigration Fees and Related Procedures Required by H.R.1 Reconciliation Bill (FR document 2026-08333), codifying H.R. 1 provisions including asylum and annual asylum fees, a Form I-94 fee and the validity period for certain employment authorization (a one-year-or-duration limit for TPS work permits per the rule excerpt); a correction followed on 2026-07-21.

DHS proposes stricter eligibility for discretionary work permits for parolees and deferred-action recipients (economic need, E-Verify employer for renewals, biometrics, generally shorter validity) and near-elimination for people on orders of supervision; comments closed 2026-08-04 with about 4,804 received.

Judge David O. Carter of the Central District of California (Jane Doe v. Department of Homeland Security, No. 8:26-cv-00060) rules that DHS did not justify issuing the 2025 interim final rule on automatic extension of work permits without notice and comment and that the rule should be set aside, with relief limited to the seven plaintiffs, per Bloomberg Law (published 2026-09-14; its headline describes an injunction while its text describes a set-aside). The court order itself was not read.

DHS publishes a final rule, effective the same day (FR document 2026-20955, RIN 1615-AD05, 91 FR 65306), adopting the October 2025 interim final rule on removal of automatic extensions of employment authorization documents without change, after 653 comment submissions.
